title: Altitude models and the hypoxic dose
goal: Name the main ways to use hypoxia, say why live high-train low exists, and compare plans by dose in km·h.

steps.title: Five ways to use hypoxia
steps.text:
All the methods share one goal: better sea-level performance [[c:mod-methods-claim]]. They differ in where you sleep, where you train and how much hypoxia you take in:

| Method | Sleep | Train | Hypoxia |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Live high–train high](g:live-high-train-high) (LHTH) | altitude | altitude | days and nights, weeks |
| [Live high–train low](g:live-high-train-low) (LHTL) | altitude, or a tent | low | nights, 12+ h·day⁻¹ |
| [Intermittent hypoxic exposure](g:intermittent-hypoxic-exposure) (IHE) | low | low | short sessions at rest |
| [Intermittent hypoxic training](g:intermittent-hypoxic-training) (IHT) | low | low, some sessions in hypoxia | during exercise |
| [Repeated-sprint training in hypoxia](g:repeated-sprint-training-in-hypoxia) (RSH) | low | low, sprint sessions in hypoxia | during sprints |

claims.text: LHTH, LHTL, IHE and IHT are distinct hypoxic methods that all aim to improve sea-level performance.

evidence.quote: Although substantial differences exist between these methods of hypoxic training and/or exposure, all have the same goal: to induce an improvement in athletic performance at sea level.

At present, several forms of hypoxic training and/or altitude exposure exist: traditional 'live high-train high' (LHTH), contemporary 'live high-train low' (LHTL), intermittent hypoxic exposure during rest (IHE) and intermittent hypoxic exposure during continuous session (IHT).

steps.title: Why live high but train low
steps.text:
Living high gives the slow adaptations (EPO, red cells). Training high costs you: the air limits your training speed. LHTL tries to keep both: acclimatise by living high, while training low to keep sea-level intensity and oxygen flow [[c:mod-lhtl-claim]].

In the 1997 trial, 39 runners did a 4-week camp: living at 2,500 m and training at 1,250 m (high–low), living and training at 2,500 m (high–high), or living and training near sea level. Both altitude groups raised VO₂max by about 5%, but 5-km time improved only in high–low, by 13.4 s [[c:mod-levine]].

claims.text: The idea of LHTL is to acclimatise while living high and keep sea-level training intensity by training low.

evidence.quote: while simultaneously allowing athletes to "train low" for the purpose of replicating sea-level training intensity and oxygen flux, thereby inducing beneficial metabolic and neuromuscular adaptations.

claims.text: In trained runners, 4 weeks of living at 2,500 m and training at 1,250 m improved 5-km time (13.4 s) while living and training at 2,500 m did not, though both raised VO₂max by about 5%.

evidence.quote: Five-kilometer time was improved by the field training camp only in the high-low group (13.4 +/- 10 s), in direct proportion to the increase in VO2 max (r = 0.65, P < 0.01).
Both altitude groups significantly increased VO2 max (5%) in direct proportion to an increase in red cell mass volume (9%; r = 0.37, P < 0.05), neither of which changed in the control.

steps.title: How much is enough: the dose
steps.text:
One research group recommends living at 2,000–2,500 m, for at least 4 weeks and at least 22 h·day⁻¹ [[c:mod-wilber]]. A review puts the minimum for red-cell effects at about 12 h·day⁻¹ [[c:mod-12h]]. In 48 runners placed at four living altitudes, 3,000-m time improved at 2,085 and 2,454 m but not at 1,780 or 2,800 m [[c:mod-chapman]].

To compare plans, add altitude and time into one number, the [hypoxic dose](g:hypoxic-dose) in kilometre-hours: altitude in km × total hours [[c:mod-kmh]].

claims.text: One research group recommends living at 2,000–2,500 m for at least 4 weeks and at least 22 h·day⁻¹ for LHTL.

evidence.quote: On the basis of consistent findings from our research group, we recommend that for athletes to derive the physiological benefits of LH+TL, they need to live at a natural elevation of 2000-2500 m for >or=4 wk for >or=22 h.d(-1).

claims.text: The minimum daily exposure for stimulating red cell production seems to be about 12 h·day⁻¹.

evidence.quote: The minimum daily dose for stimulating erythropoiesis seems to be 12 h/day.

claims.text: In runners randomised to four living altitudes, 3,000-m time improved at 2,085 and 2,454 m but not at 1,780 or 2,800 m.

evidence.quote: On return from altitude, 3,000-m time trial performance was significantly improved in groups living at the middle two altitudes (2,085 and 2,454 m), but not in groups living at 1,780 and 2,800 m.

claims.text: Hypoxic dose has been expressed in kilometre-hours: altitude in km times total hours of exposure.

evidence.quote: proposed a new metric, with hypoxic dose termed “kilometer hours” and defined as km·h (“km” denotes elevation of the exposure and “h” is the total duration of the exposure).

steps.title: Kilometre-hours of a camp
steps.problem: A camp is at 2.5 km, with 22 h·day⁻¹ of exposure for 28 days. What is the hypoxic dose?
steps: Altitude must be in km, not m; and it is the total hours, not hours per day.

steps.title: Tents and rooms: pressure vs oxygen share
steps.text:
You cannot lower the air pressure of a bedroom, but you can lower its oxygen share. A tent or room pumped with nitrogen gives [normobaric hypoxia](g:normobaric-hypoxia) at the same PIO₂ as a given altitude. Because PIO₂ is FiO₂ × (PB − 47), the FiO₂ for an altitude is:

**FiO₂ = 20.9% × (PIO₂ at altitude ÷ 150 mmHg)**

A 2,500 m tent therefore runs at about 15% oxygen. Tents make LHTL possible at home, but make sure the dose matches what you want: 8–10 h per night gives far fewer km·h than a 22 h·day⁻¹ mountain camp.

steps.title: Training in hypoxia: IHT and RSH
steps.text:
Doing sessions in hypoxia sounds like a shortcut, but a review found strikingly poor benefits from IHT for sea-level performance compared with the same training in normal air [[c:mod-iht]]. The review names a cause: hypoxia lowers the training stimulus you can produce.

RSH tries to get round that with short (under 30 s) all-out sprints and incomplete rests. A [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) of 9 controlled studies (202 people, 180 male) found mean repeated-sprint performance improved more with RSH than with sea-level sprints, but the result is borderline: P = 0.05, and the 95% [confidence interval](g:confidence-interval) just includes zero [[c:mod-rsh]]. For how each method changes VO₂max, see the paper of the week of 21 October 2026.

claims.text: A review of IHT studies found strikingly poor sea-level benefits compared with the same training in normoxia.

evidence.quote: A thorough analysis of studies including IHT, however, leads to strikingly poor benefits for sea-level performance improvement, compared to the same training method performed in normoxia.

To overcome some of the inherent limitations of IHT (lower training stimulus due to hypoxia), recent studies have successfully investigated a new training method based on the repetition of short (<30 s) 'all-out' sprints with incomplete recoveries in hypoxia, the so-called repeated sprint training in hypoxia (RSH).

claims.text: RSH improved mean repeated-sprint performance more than sea-level sprint training (SMD 0.46, 95% CI −0.02 to 0.93, P = 0.05) in 9 controlled studies.

evidence.quote: After data pooling, mean performance during repeated sprints (SMD = 0.46, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.02 to 0.93; P = 0.05) was further enhanced with RSH when compared with RSN.
After systematic review, nine controlled studies were selected, including a total of 202 individuals (mean age 22.6 ± 6.1 years; 180 males).

points: Five methods: LHTH, LHTL, IHE, IHT, RSH. They differ in where you sleep, where you train and when you breathe hypoxic air.
LHTL lets you acclimatise high and train at sea-level intensity; in the 1997 trial only the high–low group got faster though both altitude groups raised VO₂max about 5%.
One group's dose: 2,000–2,500 m, at least 4 weeks, at least 22 h·day⁻¹; the hypoxic dose in km·h is altitude (km) × total hours.
A tent copies altitude by lowering the oxygen share: about 15% at 2,500 m.
IHT showed poor sea-level benefits; RSH looks promising for repeated sprints but rests on 9 small studies whose confidence interval touches zero.

variants.stem: A cyclist sleeps 9 h a night in a tent that simulates 3,000 m and trains outdoors near sea level. Which method is this?

options.why: The training is low, so it is not live high–train high.
Correct: nights high (simulated), training low.
Exposure at rest means sitting in hypoxia, not sleeping for a night in it.
Training is not done in hypoxia here.

variants.stem: A triathlete lives and trains at a camp at 2,100 m for three weeks. Which method is this?

options.why: Correct: living and training at altitude.
Training is not at sea level: it is at the camp altitude.
No separate exposure sessions: the whole day is at altitude.
Only some sessions in hypoxia would be training in hypoxia.

variants.stem: A runner lives at sea level and wears a hypoxic mask for two interval sessions a week. Which method is this?

options.why: She does not live at altitude.
She does not sleep in hypoxia, so it is not live high–train low.
The hypoxia is during exercise, not at rest.
Correct: sessions done in hypoxia while living low.

variants.stem: A swimmer sits in a hypoxic room for 90 minutes a day at rest and lives and trains at sea level. Which method is this?

options.why: He neither lives nor trains at altitude.
Nights and living are low, so it is not live high–train low.
Correct: hypoxic air at rest while living and training low.
No training is done in hypoxia, only rest.

options.text: To keep sea-level training speed and oxygen flow, which altitude limits
options.why: Correct: it keeps training quality while living high gives the acclimatisation.

options.text: Because red cells only form when you train at sea level
options.why: Red cells respond to the hours spent living in hypoxia, not to where you train.

options.text: Because training in thin air is dangerous at any altitude
options.why: The reason is training quality, not general danger.

variants.stem: In the 1997 trial both altitude groups raised VO₂max by about 5%, but only the high–low group ran 5 km faster. What does this suggest?

options.text: A higher VO₂max is enough by itself to run faster
options.why: The high–high group raised VO₂max too and was not faster.

options.text: Training low may have kept the speed and quality that living-and-training high lost
options.why: Correct: the authors argue that sea-level training velocities were maintained in the high–low group.

options.text: Training at 1,250 m builds more red cells than living at 2,500 m
options.why: Both altitude groups raised red cell mass; the difference was in training.

variants.stem: At roughly what natural altitude does one research group advise living for LHTL?

options.why: Too low for a reliable red-cell effect in the studies cited.
Correct: the recommended altitude; a randomised study also found gains at 2,085 and 2,454 m.
Too high: the 2,800 m group in the dose study did not improve 3,000-m time.
Far above the moderate altitudes used in LHTL.

variants.stem: A cyclist sleeps in a tent simulating 2.8 km for 16 h each day for 21 days. What is the hypoxic dose in km·h?

options.why: Forgot the number of days: 2.8 × 16.
Used metres instead of kilometres.
Added the three numbers: 2.8 + 16 + 21.

variants.solution: Total hours = 16 × 21 = 336 h. Dose = 2.8 × 336 = 940.8, about 941 km·h.

variants.stem: A runner sleeps in a tent simulating 3.0 km for 10 h each night for 14 nights. What is the hypoxic dose in km·h?

options.why: Forgot the number of nights: 3.0 × 10.
Used metres instead of kilometres.
Added the three numbers: 3.0 + 10 + 14.

variants.stem: A triathlete lives at 2.0 km for 12 h each day for 28 days. What is the hypoxic dose in km·h?

options.why: Forgot the number of days: 2.0 × 12.
Used metres instead of kilometres.
Added the three numbers: 2 + 12 + 28.

variants.stem: Sea-level PIO₂ is 150 mmHg and the target altitude of 2,500 m has PIO₂ 108 mmHg. At normal pressure, about what FiO₂ should the tent have?

options.why: Divided 108 by the barometric pressure 760, ignoring the water vapour.
Left the oxygen share unchanged: that is sea-level air.
Turned the ratio upside down: 20.9 ÷ 0.72.

variants.stem: Sea-level PIO₂ is 150 mmHg and the target altitude of 3,000 m has PIO₂ 101 mmHg. At normal pressure, about what FiO₂ should the tent have?

options.why: Divided 101 by the barometric pressure 760, ignoring the water vapour.
Turned the ratio upside down: 20.9 ÷ 0.67.
Left the oxygen share unchanged: that is sea-level air.

variants.stem: Sea-level PIO₂ is 150 mmHg and the target altitude of 4,000 m has PIO₂ 87 mmHg. At normal pressure, about what FiO₂ should the room have?

options.why: Divided 87 by the barometric pressure 760, ignoring the water vapour.
Turned the ratio upside down: 20.9 ÷ 0.58.
Left the oxygen share unchanged: that is sea-level air.

variants.stem: Why was RSH proposed as an alternative to IHT?

options.text: Hypoxia lowers the training stimulus in IHT; short all-out sprints keep it high
options.why: Correct: the review names the lower stimulus as the limit of IHT.

options.text: Sprints are done at higher altitude than IHT, so hypoxia is stronger
options.why: The point is the stimulus, not a higher altitude.

options.text: IHT is banned in team sports but RSH is not
options.why: Nothing in the review concerns bans.

variants.stem: RSH vs sea-level sprints: SMD 0.46, 95% CI −0.02 to 0.93, P = 0.05, in 9 studies with 202 people (180 male). What conclusion fits?

options.text: RSH is proven to beat normal sprint training in all athletes
options.why: The interval includes zero and few studies were pooled.

options.text: There is no effect, because the interval touches zero
options.why: Zero is only just inside the interval; a likely small-to-moderate benefit is not ruled out.

options.text: A benefit is plausible but uncertain, and the data are mainly from men
options.why: Correct: borderline result, few studies, 90% male.
